texts: mixed: the Council, the approval, the beneficiary and the date all land, but "at the Harbor Station" is hung on the approving event, so the parse says the Council did its approving at the station rather than that the approved half-shifts are there; and "day 80 of Year 1" fills the day-of-month slot, so it records the 80th of a month. If the station is where the shifts are, give that its own clause: "On day 80 of Year 1, the Council approved half-shifts for Coraline Ash. The half-shifts were at the Harbor Station." A day-of-year count has no faithful slot in our time terms, so if your calendar has month names, date the episode as a month plus a day within it.
good. the retirement, the resulting unstaffed station, the "so" link and the ordering between the two past-perfect clauses all come through.

mixed: the lighting, the lantern's link to the station and "at sundown" all land, but "for the first time" is dropped silently — there is no slot for an occasion count on a one-off event, so the parse records an ordinary lighting with no first-occasion claim at all. Put that claim in its own finite clause: "Coraline Ash lit the lantern of the Harbor Station at sundown. She had not lit it before."
good. "stood beside" is recorded as a plain past position relation between Pell and Coraline Ash, with no invented event.

mixed: the catching, its manner and the wick itself all land, but the parse also links the wick to the lantern on an inference your words never state, and our instruction set points both ways on whether that link may be emitted — so the same sentence can parse two ways from one run to the next. Put the link in the words: "The lantern's wick caught cleanly."
good. the burning, the lantern as what burns and mire-essence as what is consumed all land, with mire-essence typed as a kind of essence.
good. the producing lands, and the mist-light gets its own referent, which is what lets the next sentence refer back to the same light.
good. the mist-light is the drawer, the nightmoths are a group whose members are left unchanged, and the moth kind is typed.
good. the landing, the lantern as the place and "after sundown" as a lower time bound all land.

bad: the threads are put in the slot for objects the action changes, but they are only deposited unaltered, so a question asking what was left on the lantern will not match the parse. Nothing in your wording caused this — the sentence is fine as written and the fix belongs on the translator's side; if you want to steer it anyway, "The nightmoth deposited silken threads on the lantern." cues the unchanged-object reading.

mixed: the two joinings did come out as two separate events, which is what the sentence means, but a pair of coordinated time phrases on one verb is territory our instruction set does not cover — one event carrying both times would have been a contradiction, so the split was an improvisation rather than a rule and may not repeat. Write one finite clause per occasion: "Pell joined Coraline Ash at the Harbor Station at midnight, and he joined her at the third watch."
